bibl.title: On Admonition and on Evil Passions Which Destroy Pure Prayer.
ܥܠ ܡܪܬܝܢܘܬܐ ܘܥܠ ܚܫܐ ܒܝܫܐ ܡܒܛܠܝ ܨܠܘܬܐ ܕܟܝܬܐ
bibl.author: Dadishoʿ Qatraya — ܕܕܝܫܘܥ ܩܛܪܝܐ

noteGrp.note: A late seventh-century East-Syriac monastic and mystical work. It describes the solitary’s progress toward pure prayer and identifies four passions that obstruct it—gluttony, excessive sleep, anger, and vainglory—and four opposing virtues: fasting, vigils, meekness, and humility. The work offers a concise account of Dadisho’s ascetic understanding of the purification of body and soul as the path to pure prayer and contemplation.

note.quote: ܙܕܩ ܠܗ ܗܟܝܠ ܠܝܚܝܕܝܐ ܕܘܡܪ ܚܕܬܐܝܬ ܒܫܠܝܐ: ܝܬܝܪ ܡܢ ܟܠ ܡܕܡ ܗܕܐ ܠܡܕܥ ܕܡܢ ܟܕ ܥܐܠ ܠܫܠܝܐ ܘܥܕܡܐ ܕܡܛܐ ܠܨܠܘܬܐ ܕܟܝܬܐ:ܕܒܐܝܕܗ ܡܬܐܣܝܢ ܚܫܘܗܝ: ܘܒܗ ܡܬܚܣܝܢ ܟܠܗܘܢ ܚܛܗܘܗܝ: ܘܡܢܗ ܥܙܠ ܠܕܟܝܘܬ ܠܒܐ ܘܠܕܘܒܪܐ ܕܪܘܝܢܐ ܘܠܪܢܝܐ ܕܒܐܠܗܐ: ܘܡܢܗ ܡܫܬܘܐ ܠܕܘܒܪܐ ܪܘܚܢܝܐ: ܕܗܠܝܢ ܐܪܒܥܐ ܚܫܐ ܡܩܪܒܝܢ ܥܡܗ ܝܬܝܪ ܡܢ ܟܠܗܘܢ ܚܫܐ.

The solitary who has only begun to live in solitude must know before anything else that, from the time he embraces solitude till the time he reaches the pure prayer, through which his passions are healed and his sins forgiven, through which he acquires purity of heart, exercise of the mind and contemplation of God, and through which he becomes worthy of the spiritual exercise—four passions fight against him more than all other passions.
The virtues of which I spoke above are: fasting, vigils, humility and meekness; and the passions contrary to them are: gluttony, excessive sleep, vainglory and anger.
